doc.title: Bobby Johnson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: His mother's speakeasy and the path to New York
summary: His mother ran a speakeasy in prohibition days, which explains how he met so many musicians, and the family ended up in New York.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Now I understand your mother owned a speakeasy, or a restaurant?

Oh yeah. Well that’s true. That’s the reason why I knew so many musicians. During those days, this was during the days of prohibition. And each town, like the high sheriff or whoever, you could get into his pocket, he would allow one speakeasy on a certain side of town. And we had just one. I lived on the east side of Pensacola. But sometimes I don’t particularly care too much about it, but Pensacola I could say that it wasn’t a Jim Crow town, it was like, I lived, to be frank with you, I came up in an exclusive white neighborhood. But we ran a speakeasy that had all kinds of clientele. And we got away with it. But when the Volstead Act came along, that was prohibition you know, President Roosevelt, we tried to get a liquor license and we couldn’t get it, and we found ourselves in New York. Now the way this happened, maybe you’ve heard of a famous clarinet player named Edmond Hall.
